idiom_name: Servlet HttpSession managed by the container (StandardManager, in-memory)
implementation_notes: The classic Java realization is the container's own session manager: HttpServletRequest.getSession() returns an HttpSession whose getId/setAttribute/getAttribute/invalidate API is the record access path, and Tomcat's standard org.apache.catalina.session.StandardManager keeps those records in memory, optionally serialising them to SESSIONS.ser across a restart. That replaces the classic role structure with a container-provided API, and the container owns identifier generation (SessionIdGenerator, configurable secureRandomAlgorithm), the maximum inactive interval and expiry frequency. It is the right default for a single node or a replicated cluster, but every attribute must be Serializable before it can survive replication or persistence, and the records are gone if the node dies without a cluster.
pitfalls: In-memory sessions have no failover story of their own: without clustering or a persistent store they vanish with the node, and the standard manager's SESSIONS.ser only covers clean restarts.
Non-serializable attributes (JDBC connections, thread-bound objects, lazy ORM proxies) break the moment the session is replicated or persisted - keep only Serializable values in the record.
Container limits are real failure modes: maxActiveSessions exhaustion makes getSession() throw IllegalStateException, and URL-based id propagation exposes identifiers in logs and referrers.

variants.name: Tomcat PersistentManager with a database or file Store
variants.implementation_notes: Same HttpSession API, different owner of the record: swapping StandardManager for org.apache.catalina.session.PersistentManager and nesting a <Store> lets Tomcat swap idle sessions into a database (DataSourceStore over a tomcat_sessions-style table whose columns hold id, serialized data, validity flag, max-inactive and last-access) or into files, and to save every session across a restart. Choose it when conversations must survive deployments and a shared database already exists; maxIdleBackup and maxIdleSwap are the tuning surface, saveOnRestart controls the shutdown path, and the store's schema and retention become your responsibility.
pitfalls: PersistentManager only works with activity checking enabled (ACTIVITY_CHECK or STRICT_SERVLET_COMPLIANCE), which is easy to miss and produces silently wrong swap behaviour.

Attributes are serialized on the way to the store, so sessionAttributeNameFilter/sessionAttributeValueClassNameFilter decide what survives; a filter that blocks a class drops it without a request-time error.
The file-based FileStore is documented as unsuited to many sessions - it exists for experiments, not for production load.

variants.name: Spring Session with a Redis or JDBC SessionRepository
variants.idiom_name: Spring Session @EnableRedisHttpSession / SessionRepository behind the same HttpSession API
variants.implementation_notes: Spring Session decouples the conversation from the container: the same HttpSession API (or Spring WebFlux's WebSession) is served by a SessionRepository backed by Redis, a relational database or another store, so the in-memory-versus-shared decision becomes configuration - @EnableRedisHttpSession, spring.session.store-type - instead of code, and REST clients can carry the session id in a header rather than a cookie. It is the variant that removes sticky sessions in a cluster and adds cross-context session sharing; the reference documents a Java 17+ baseline and (for the Redis index) Redis 2.8+ so that session expiration works.
pitfalls: The backing store joins the critical path of every authenticated request: an unreachable Redis makes the application unable to resolve sessions, so timeouts and a failure policy are required.
Attributes need a serialization strategy that tolerates application upgrades (JDK serialization ties records to class versions; JSON needs explicit types).
Retention is store-specific: Redis keys must carry a TTL through the index, JDBC stores need their own cleanup, and a misconfigured TTL quietly turns sessions immortal.
